paper.title: Immune evasion in Mucorales species: From stealth spores to angioinvasive hyphae
paper.abstract: Mucormycosis is an invasive fungal infection caused by members of the order Mucorales, which employ stage- and species-specific mechanisms to evade host immunity. Resting spores of experimentally studied Rhizopus species can persist after macrophage uptake because macrophages restrict germination but do not efficiently kill all internalized resting spores. Germination is accompanied by cell-wall remodeling and increased β-glucan exposure in several experimentally examined Mucorales species; however, functional Dectin-1-dependent responses have been demonstrated most clearly in Rhizopus and its conservation across species and isolates remains incompletely defined. Studies predominantly in Rhizopus delemar identify fungal CotH proteins as ligands for host GRP78 or integrin α3β1, linking invasion to tissue-specific host pathways. Intracellular survival also varies across species: Rhizopus spores remain dormant and prevent phagosome maturation, whereas Mucor circinelloides can germinate within macrophages via stress-response and calcineurin-dependent mechanisms. Cunninghamella shows a significant resistance to neutrophil damage, while other Mucorales species suppress accumulation of nitric oxide in activated macrophages. Studies of Rhizopus reveal morphology-dependent dendritic-cell activation and Th17 polarization, and that Rhizopus-specific T cells can directly damage fungal hyphae. Whether such adaptive responses are present in other Mucorales species remains unknown. Understanding these immune evasion mechanisms could support the development of therapies focused on cytokines, adoptive T-cells, and CotH-targets.
